extracted.intended_audience: historical demographers, ethnohistorians, and anthropologists studying California indigenous population history
extracted.subtask_description: Methods and standards for estimating precontact and early-19th-century native populations in the San Joaquin/Merced/Kings river regions using documentary, mission, and geographic/area-based evidence, with corrections for reporting biases and attrition. Focuses on combining direct counts, indirect inferences, and cross-checks to arrive at plausible population totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by multiple independent accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Give weight to villages or rancherias that are mentioned independently by at least two writers; treat those as reliably attested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'six rancherias, each of which is mentioned independently by at least two writers' (used to identify Cheneches, Malim, Nupchenches, Cutucho, Copicha, Tape). Use independent mentions as a baseline for including a village in counts; treat single-source mentions with more caution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum-population inference from captive counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Infer minimum population sizes from counts of captives or prisoners reported by explorers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Pico's capture of '100 warriors and 300 of all ages and sexes' used to ascribe a minimum of 300 to a rancheria. Use captive tallies as lower bounds rather than precise totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inferring human population from animal counts (horse-meat/horse counts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use counts of animals (live and dead horses/mules) observed at sites and along routes to infer population supporting/consuming them, via assumed ratios of animals per person or per community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: At Tape 254 animals counted and 500 dead horses from Tape to Cheneches; applying previously discussed dead-horse-to-inhabitants ratio yielded an estimate of ~2,500 persons for the villages in that segment. Must justify that the animals were consumed by the entire group rather than a subset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riverbank-distance proportionality (persons per river mile)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume villages are spaced uniformly along larger rivers and therefore use river-mileage to estimate population, producing a persons-per-river-mile metric.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Airline river lengths used; divide region into river sectors (e.g., lower Merced, middle Kings, lower Kings), compute persons per river mile (e.g., 55, 67, 75) and take a mean (~65) to extrapolate to other streams. Beware of local variation and meanders; use only when habitat and settlement patterns are broadly uniform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of river sectors and airline distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Define river sectors and use airline (straight-line) distances as proxies for stream length when streams are substantially straight, to compute persons-per-mile.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justification: 'The general course of all the streams is substantially straight and the numerous small meanders are uniform in size and occurrence.' Partition the study area into sectors and tabulate miles, population, and persons per river mile.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt or transfer average village sizes from comparable areas/periods
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct counts are lacking, adopt an average persons-per-village from comparable regions or periods (e.g., 60, 100, 150, 300) depending on whether data are for reduced (post-contact) or aboriginal/precontact times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Gifford's average of 21 (used for some calculations), 60 for 1850-era reduced villages, or 150 for estimated precontact village size. Choose the average consistent with evidence of reduction/attrition and contextual similarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply reduction/attrition correction factors to observed later counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust observed population figures from later periods (e.g., 1850) upward to estimate aboriginal/precontact populations by applying an estimated reduction percentage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 1850 total (3,900) represented 32.5% of the estimated aboriginal population -> implies aboriginal total ~12,000 for certain regions. Use documented evidence of depopulation (massacres, epidemics, raids) to estimate reduction factor; document assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mission baptism records to identify origin villages and timing of depopulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use baptism books (village name + date of baptism) from missions to trace which villages were cleaned out by a given date and to identify villages originating from the central valley vs. foothill tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If baptisms from a village appear only after 1805 and names do not match ethnographers' known villages, infer central valley origin and that the village was 'cleaned out' before 1805. Use San Francisco, San Jose, Santa Clara mission records as critical sources but account for possible overlaps and mission founding dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust for recorder/counting method differences (age/sex cutoffs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Correct raw counts to a common basis because different recorders used different age cutoffs and definitions of 'men' and 'children' (e.g., Zalvidea counted males from age 7; Franciscans used age 10).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Zalvidea's method required converting his 'men' counts into total population by adding children proportionally (he counted everyone >7 as male or female). Use established percentage breakdowns (e.g., men 41.8%, women 41.8%, children 16.4% from mission data) to standardize counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: House-count to persons-per-house conversion
rubrics_metrics.description: Use number of houses and ethnographic/structural data about house size to estimate persons per house and thus total village population.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Tauquimenes with 60 houses -> 9.38 persons/house; Chuppumne's large houses (40–50 paces circumference) plausibly accommodated ~9 persons. Use physical dimensions and comparable examples to justify persons-per-house values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Route reconstruction and spatial inference from explorers' itineraries
rubrics_metrics.description: Plot the explorer's reported leagues, directions, and campsite descriptions on maps to locate rancherias and count how many villages were seen along certain river reaches or creeks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Use Garces' described legs (leagues and directions) to place rancherias nos.1–12, infer which were on Kern/Poso/White rivers, and assess which stretches were not visited and thus undercounted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'rancherias despobladas' and signs of permanent depopulation
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiate between temporarily deserted villages (inhabitants in hiding) and 'rancherias despobladas' implying permanent abandonment due to warfare, disease, or removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Garces' observation of permanently depopulated rancherias suggests early onset of decline; incorporate such qualitative notes into decisions about extrapolating unseen villages and timing of depopulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile and average differing estimates from direct documentary and indirect methods
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct documentary (explorer counts) and indirect metric methods (river-mile extrapolation) diverge, consider both and use an average or reasoned compromise as a 'fair figure'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Garces direct estimate 2,400 vs. river-mile indirect 3,000 -> take the mean (2,700) as a reasonable estimate. Always record the two sources and justify the averaging approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Area-based density checks with stated uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: Validate population totals by computing population density per square mile for major regions and comparing densities across similar physiographic regions; state an error margin for area calculations (e.g., ±20%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Block out four major regions, compute area and population density (e.g., Kaweah-Tulare 7.12 per sq. mi.), and compare densities to check plausibility. Note sources of discrepancy (uninhabitable mountain areas, incomplete lower-river reporting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust for author/reporting bias and incompleteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize specific tendencies of historical writers (e.g., Moraga tended to underestimate and omitted villages) and account for likely omissions when aggregating documentary evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Where Moraga records fewer villages or smaller numbers, consider that his reports may undercount settlements; complement with other observers and indirect methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of later informant village lists to estimate earlier village numbers cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: When early records are sparse, use village lists collected from informants by later ethnographers (Kroeber, Latta) to estimate minimum village counts in earlier periods, with caution about memory and temporal mismatch.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Kroeber and Latta identified 36 villages for seven tribes based on informants; accept that as a plausible minimum for 1800 but note uncertainties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Back-calculation from warrior counts to total population
rubrics_metrics.description: Convert reported numbers of warriors engaged in battle to total village population by accounting for non-combatant males (boys, old men, invalids) and expected warrior fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Soto's reported 1,000 warriors from four rancherias is probably high; halving the estimate to 500 warriors and adding estimated non-combatant males yields a male population estimate (e.g., 800), which then scales to a total village size using mission-derived percentages (arriving at ~475 mean village). Use conservative reductions and document assumptions.
